prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock, based on trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, and for its realisation at the 10^-18 level through control of systematic and collective shifts

statement.case_for: I keep B051 as my preferred prize, and I have tested that against the full round-1 exchange rather than against the support count. The scientific core is unchanged. Katori's magic-wavelength condition removes the lattice light shift on the clock transition and lets thousands of neutral atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime at once, so the statistical advantage of an ensemble is combined with the freedom from Doppler and recoil shifts that single ions have. That is a different principle from the 2005 comb, which supplied the ruler that counts optical cycles, and from the 2012 work, which controlled one quantum system at a time. Ye's group then showed that the many-atom advantage survives: they reached the 10^-18 level, and in doing so identified and controlled density-dependent, collective and blackbody shifts that would otherwise have capped the approach. As a many-body theorist I regard that second step as physics and not only engineering, because the error budget became a many-body problem. The result is reproduced across laboratories and species and enters international comparisons, so maturity is not in question. The credit is two names with no forced cut. The round-1 exchange sharpened one thing for me: the citation must be written narrowly around the lattice clock concept and its realisation, so that it claims neither optical metrology as a whole nor the territory of earlier prizes.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection is still the strongest one: a critic can read the lattice clock as an outstanding refinement of the 2005 and 2012 toolboxes, and Eriksson, Olsson and Pearce all say so in their own words. Ion-clock groups, the ultrastable-laser work and other lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Kimble) are not credited, and the opening base for B051 is the narrowest of the leading candidates. I also accept that B050 offers a broader conceptual reach across condensed matter, which Kroll's criterion question puts fairly: a new organising principle against a new level of accuracy. My honest assessment is that the clock is the stronger candidate on attribution and the weaker on breadth, and that reasonable members can weigh those differently. Finally, my own field proximity may be inflating my view of how new the lattice step is, which is why I want the novelty argument stated openly and not assumed.

responses.point: Danielsson asks whether Ye's contribution can be described as more than engineering excellence, and notes that our views of B050's depth may not differ on substance, only in how to weigh a concept against an instrument.
responses.response: I think it can, and this is the part of the credit I would defend most firmly. The question Ye's group answered was not only how to reduce noise but whether a many-atom lattice clock could keep its accuracy at all once the atoms interact and the lattice, the blackbody environment and the probe laser each shift the line. Establishing that collective and density-dependent shifts can be measured, modelled and suppressed to 10^-18 is what turned Katori's proposal into a clock that competes with and surpasses single ions. On your second point, I agree that we do not disagree on the depth of B050. Where we differ is the criterion, and I have not claimed that an instrument outranks a concept in general; I claim that here the instrument embodies a new principle and has a clean credit.

responses.point: Eriksson reads B050 as a conceptual reorganisation of a field and B051 as a superb refinement of an established metrology programme, and says he would turn to B051 if the BHZ credit proves indefensible.
responses.response: The refinement reading is the one I most need to answer, and I do not think it fits the facts. A refinement improves a known scheme; the magic-wavelength lattice changed what the oscillator is, by trading a single trapped particle for an ensemble held without light shift, and the many-body-limited error budget has no counterpart in the 2005 or 2012 work. I accept that this is argued and not self-evident, and that is why the citation should state it. I note your fallback with interest: if the committee agrees that the BHZ omission is a defect in the prize itself, as I think it is, then the choice is not close to a tie, because B051 has no comparable gap in its credit. I would still not oppose B050 if the committee can settle that question, and I will not use the redefinition of the second as a reason to prefer either.

responses.point: Kroll frames the choice between B050 and B051 as a conceptual organising principle against a new level of accuracy, and asks the committee to decide which it rates higher, while urging a citation written narrowly around the lattice clock.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and with the narrow citation, which is why my revised wording names the magic-wavelength trapping and the 10^-18 realisation and says nothing about optical metrology generally. On the criterion I would add that the two are not exclusive here: a new level of accuracy is the visible result, but the reason it was reachable is a conceptual step, and I think the committee should avoid describing the clock as accuracy alone. Where I am more cautious than you is on the shared proximity. We both come from fields near this one, so if the committee judges that proximity material I would want the others to weigh our confidence accordingly, and I would not object to that.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved to B050 for its prediction-then-experiment structure and asks that the committee decide the redefinition of the second explicitly and not by default.
responses.response: I accept your request, and my position is explicit: the pending redefinition is not a reason to wait, because the clocks are reproduced in many laboratories and compared internationally, so the physics does not depend on a metrological decision. If the committee prefers to wait, it should record that as a judgement. I agree that B050 has the cleaner prediction-then-experiment story. My disagreement is with calling it the safer choice on credit: the structure is clean, but the people who proposed the HgTe route that the experiment tested are outside the three names, and a careful citation cannot hide that.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Lindroth's fourth place for B050 reflects doubt about the science or only distance from the field, and says she does not see B051 as stronger on originality and breadth of influence.
responses.response: It reflects distance from the field and not doubt about the science. I regard the Kane-Mele Z2 classification and the HgTe edge conductance as established, and that is why B050 is my first alternative and not a candidate I would block. My reservation is about the credit and about how I weigh breadth against a clean attribution, not about whether the effect exists. On originality I would put the magic-wavelength lattice at least on a par with a single insight of this kind, but I accept your point that its breadth of influence on other fields is narrower, and that a committee valuing breadth would reasonably prefer B050.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that lattice simulation changed how many-body problems are posed while clocks act on other physics mainly through tests and applications, and says he would not oppose B051 if the committee wants a cleaner credit.
responses.response: I take the point on breadth for the clocks, and I would add that the same difficulty you name for B027 is the reason I cannot support it this year: five names are cut to three, Greiner and Dalibard are left out, and Cirac and Zoller are also in B015. Those are credit problems, not doubts about the science. On impact, I would say the clocks are not only a measuring instrument: the collective-shift physics they exposed is a many-body problem in its own right, and tests of fundamental constants are physics, not only application. But I accept that this is a narrower reach than yours, and I am glad you would not oppose B051.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct principle from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or reads it as a refinement; I think the citation has to make this case itself.
Whether the committee should wait for the formal redefinition of the second; I do not think so, but I want the decision recorded explicitly.

Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission can be defended for B050; if the committee judges it can, I would move to accept B050 as a close call, and if not, I regard B051 as clearly better on attribution.
Whether the committee prefers a new conceptual organising principle with a contested credit or a metrological advance with a clean credit, and how much my own field proximity affects my weighing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is documented for Katori or Ye. My collaborations (Lund and ETH attosecond groups, L'Huillier, Keller, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) do not include either of them. I am a theoretical atomic physicist and my field proximity to precision atomic spectroscopy is a source of bias, which I disclose, not a formal conflict. I have no documented tie to any credited name in B050 or B015, my alternatives. I would accept the committee's judgement if it considered my proximity material.
